subject: maths
title: Primary 4 Area and Perimeter
seo_title: P4 Area and Perimeter Worksheets: Free Primary 4 Maths with Answers (MOE Syllabus)
standard_text: Finding one dimension of a rectangle given its area/perimeter; side of a square from its area/perimeter; area and perimeter of composite figures made of rectangles and squares
meta_desc: Free P4 area and perimeter practice: missing length or breadth, sides of squares, composite figures and word problems. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Missing breadth from a perimeter of 30 cm and a length of 9 cm: 30 ÷ 2 = 15, then 15 − 9 = 6 cm.
body_html:
Area and perimeter

Area is the space inside a figure. It is measured in square units: cm² or m². Perimeter is the distance all round the edge. It is a length: cm or m.

For a square, area = side × side and perimeter = 4 × side.

Find the length or breadth

Know the area? Divide: missing side = area ÷ the side you know.

Know the perimeter? First halve it. Half the perimeter is length + breadth.

Example

A rectangle has a perimeter of 30 cm. Its length is 9 cm. Find its breadth.

Length + breadth = 30 ÷ 2 = 15 cm. Breadth = 15 − 9 = 6 cm.

Answer: 6 cm

The side of a square

From the perimeter: divide by 4. From the area: find the number that times itself gives the area. Use your multiplication tables.

Example

A square has a perimeter of 32 cm. What is its area?

Side = 32 ÷ 4 = 8 cm. Area = 8 × 8 = 64 cm².

Answer: 64 cm²

Composite figures

A composite figure is made of rectangles and squares. Find the missing sides first: the sides going one way add up to the side across from them. For the area, split the figure into rectangles and add. For the perimeter, add every side of the outline.

Word problems

A fence, a border or a ribbon goes round the edge: find the perimeter. Tiles, carpet, paint or grass cover the inside: find the area.

Model method

The length of a rectangle is 3 times its breadth. Its perimeter is 64 cm. Find its area.

Length + breadth = 64 ÷ 2 = 32 cm = 4 units. 1 unit = 8 cm. Breadth = 8 cm, length = 24 cm. Area = 24 × 8 = 192 cm².

Answer: 192 cm²

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Mixing up area and perimeterInside: area, in cm² or m². Round the edge: perimeter, in cm or m
Adding only one length and one breadthPerimeter = 2 × (length + breadth)
30 − 9 = 21 for the breadthHalve the perimeter first: 30 ÷ 2 = 15, then 15 − 9 = 6
Halving the area to find a side (48 ÷ 2)Divide by the side you know: 48 ÷ 8 = 6
49 ÷ 4 for the side of a square of area 49 cm²Find the number that times itself gives 49: 7
Using a whole side for a part in a composite figureWork out the part first: 8 − 3 = 5 cm

faq.q: What is taught in P4 area and perimeter?
faq.a: Primary 4 students find the length or breadth of a rectangle from its area or perimeter, the side of a square from its area or perimeter, and the area and perimeter of composite figures made of rectangles and squares.

faq.q: How do I find the breadth of a rectangle from its perimeter?
faq.a: Halve the perimeter to get length + breadth, then take away the length. For a perimeter of 30 cm and a length of 9 cm: 30 ÷ 2 = 15, and 15 − 9 = 6 cm.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake in area and perimeter?
faq.a: Mixing up the two: area is the space inside (cm², m²) and perimeter is the distance round (cm, m). Another is forgetting to halve the perimeter before finding a missing side.

faq.q: Is area and perimeter in the MOE syllabus for Primary 4?
faq.a: Yes. It is part of Area and Volume in Measurement and Geometry. It builds on P3 area and perimeter and prepares for the area of triangles in P5 and circles in P6, which come up in the PSLE.

sets.title: Area and perimeter of rectangles and squares

items.q: What is the area of this rectangle?
items.e: Area = length × breadth = 9 × 6 = 54 cm². (30 cm is the perimeter, 9 + 6 = 15 only adds two sides, and 108 doubles the area.)

items.q: What is the area of this rectangle?
items.e: Area = length × breadth = 12 × 5 = 60 m². (34 m is the perimeter, 12 + 5 = 17 only adds two sides, and 120 doubles the area.)

items.q: What is the area of this rectangle?
items.e: Area = length × breadth = 8 × 7 = 56 cm². (30 cm is the perimeter, 8 + 7 = 15 only adds two sides, and 112 doubles the area.)

items.q: What is the perimeter of this rectangle?
items.e: Perimeter = 2 × (length + breadth) = 2 × (11 + 4) = 2 × 15 = 30 cm. (15 cm goes only halfway round; 11 × 4 = 44 is the area.)

items.q: What is the perimeter of this rectangle?
items.e: Perimeter = 2 × (length + breadth) = 2 × (15 + 6) = 2 × 21 = 42 m. (21 m goes only halfway round; 15 × 6 = 90 is the area.)

items.q: What is the perimeter of this rectangle?
items.e: Perimeter = 2 × (length + breadth) = 2 × (13 + 8) = 2 × 21 = 42 cm. (21 cm goes only halfway round; 13 × 8 = 104 is the area.)

items.q: A rectangular poster has a length of 24 cm and a breadth of 15 cm. What is its area?
items.e: Area = 24 × 15. 24 × 10 = 240 and 24 × 5 = 120. 240 + 120 = 360 cm². (144 comes from writing 24 × 1 instead of 24 × 10.)

items.q: A rectangular car park has a length of 35 m and a breadth of 18 m. What is its area?
A school field has a length of 125 m and a breadth of 80 m. What is its perimeter?
items.e: 2 × (125 + 80) = 2 × 205 = 410 m. (205 m goes only halfway round, 330 m leaves out one breadth, and 125 × 80 = 10 000 is the area.)

items.q: A rectangular table top has a length of 1 m and a breadth of 45 cm. What is its perimeter in centimetres?
items.e: Change to one unit first: 1 m = 100 cm. 2 × (100 + 45) = 2 × 145 = 290 cm. (92 comes from 2 × (1 + 45), mixing metres and centimetres.)

items.q: A square has sides of 9 cm. What is its area?
items.e: Area of a square = side × side = 9 × 9 = 81 cm². (4 × 9 = 36 is the perimeter; 72 is 9 × 8, a slip in the multiplication table.)

items.q: A square has sides of 14 m. What is its perimeter?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides: 4 × 14 = 56 m. (14 × 14 = 196 is the area; 28 m and 42 m count only 2 or 3 sides.)

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm by 1 cm. What is the area of the shaded rectangle?
items.e: 4 rows of 7 squares: 4 × 7 = 28 squares, so the area is 28 cm². (22 cm is the perimeter; 18 counts only the squares along the edge.)

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm by 1 cm. What is the perimeter of the shaded rectangle?
items.e: Count the 1-cm sides all round: 6 + 5 + 6 + 5 = 22 cm. (30 is the number of squares, the area. 18 counts the edge squares, but each corner square has two sides on the edge.)

items.q: Which unit is best for the area of a classroom floor?
items.e: Area is the space inside, so it needs a square unit. A floor is big, so use square metres, m².

items.q: Which unit is best for the length of ribbon round the edge of a birthday card?
items.e: Ribbon round the edge is a perimeter, so it needs a length unit. A card is small, so use centimetres.

items.q: Which gives the perimeter of a rectangle?
items.e: Perimeter is the distance round: 2 lengths and 2 breadths, which is 2 × (length + breadth). length × breadth is the area.

items.q: Which gives the area of a rectangle?
items.e: Area counts the unit squares inside: rows × squares in each row = length × breadth.

items.q: Rectangle A is 9 cm by 4 cm. Rectangle B is a square with sides of 6 cm. Both have an area of 36 cm². Which has the longer perimeter?
items.e: A: 2 × (9 + 4) = 26 cm. B: 4 × 6 = 24 cm. 26 − 24 = 2, so A is longer by 2 cm. The same area does not mean the same perimeter.

items.q: Which rectangle has an area of 24 cm²?
items.e: 6 × 4 = 24 cm². (8 cm by 4 cm has a perimeter of 24 cm, not an area of 24 cm². 20 + 4 and 12 + 12 add to 24, but area means multiplying.)

items.q: The area of the rectangle is 40 cm². What is its breadth?
items.e: Area = length × breadth, so 8 × ? = 40. 40 ÷ 8 = 5. The breadth is 5 cm. Check: 8 × 5 = 40. (Subtracting, 40 − 8 = 32, is a common mistake.)

items.q: The area of the rectangle is 54 m². What is its breadth?
items.e: Area = length × breadth, so 9 × ? = 54. 54 ÷ 9 = 6. The breadth is 6 m. Check: 9 × 6 = 54. (Subtracting, 54 − 9 = 45, is a common mistake.)

items.q: The area of the rectangle is 36 cm². What is its breadth?
items.e: Area = length × breadth, so 9 × ? = 36. 36 ÷ 9 = 4. The breadth is 4 cm. Check: 9 × 4 = 36. (Subtracting, 36 − 9 = 27, is a common mistake.)

items.q: The area of the rectangle is 60 m². What is its length?
items.e: Area = length × breadth, so 5 × ? = 60. 60 ÷ 5 = 12. The length is 12 m. Check: 5 × 12 = 60. (Subtracting, 60 − 5 = 55, is a common mistake.)

items.q: The area of the rectangle is 78 cm². What is its length?
items.e: Area = length × breadth, so 6 × ? = 78. 78 ÷ 6 = 13. The length is 13 cm. Check: 6 × 13 = 78. (Subtracting, 78 − 6 = 72, is a common mistake.)

items.q: A rectangle has an area of 96 cm². Its breadth is 8 cm. What is its length?
items.e: Length = area ÷ breadth = 96 ÷ 8 = 12 cm. Check: 12 × 8 = 96 cm².

items.q: A rectangle has an area of 126 m². Its breadth is 9 m. What is its length?
items.e: Length = area ÷ breadth = 126 ÷ 9 = 14 m. Check: 14 × 9 = 126 m².

items.q: A rectangle has an area of 150 cm². Its breadth is 10 cm. What is its length?
items.e: Length = area ÷ breadth = 150 ÷ 10 = 15 cm. Check: 15 × 10 = 150 cm².

items.q: A rectangle has an area of 168 m². Its breadth is 7 m. What is its length?
items.e: Length = area ÷ breadth = 168 ÷ 7 = 24 m. Check: 24 × 7 = 168 m².

items.q: The perimeter of the rectangle is 30 cm. What is its breadth?
items.e: Half the perimeter is length + breadth: 30 ÷ 2 = 15 cm. Breadth = 15 − 9 = 6 cm. (30 − 9 − 9 = 12 is two breadths, so it still needs halving.)

items.q: A rectangle has a perimeter of 40 m. Its length is 12 m. What is its breadth?
items.e: Half the perimeter is length + breadth: 40 ÷ 2 = 20 m. Breadth = 20 − 12 = 8 m. (40 − 12 − 12 = 16 is two breadths, so it still needs halving.)

items.q: A rectangle has a perimeter of 54 cm. Its length is 15 cm. What is its breadth?
items.e: Half the perimeter is length + breadth: 54 ÷ 2 = 27 cm. Breadth = 27 − 15 = 12 cm. (54 − 15 − 15 = 24 is two breadths, so it still needs halving.)

items.q: The perimeter of the rectangle is 36 cm. What is its length?
items.e: Half the perimeter is length + breadth: 36 ÷ 2 = 18 cm. Length = 18 − 7 = 11 cm. (36 − 7 − 7 = 22 is two lengths, so it still needs halving.)

items.q: A rectangle has a perimeter of 70 m. Its length is 20 m. What is its breadth?
items.e: Half the perimeter is length + breadth: 70 ÷ 2 = 35 m. Breadth = 35 − 20 = 15 m. (70 − 20 − 20 = 30 is two breadths, so it still needs halving.)

items.q: A rectangle has a perimeter of 54 cm. What is its length + breadth?
items.e: The perimeter is 2 lengths + 2 breadths. Half of it is 1 length + 1 breadth: 54 ÷ 2 = 27 cm. (13.5 cm divides by 4, as for a square.)

items.q: The length + breadth of a rectangle is 19 m. What is its perimeter?
items.e: Perimeter = 2 × (length + breadth) = 2 × 19 = 38 m. (76 m multiplies by 4, as for a square.)

items.q: A rectangle has an area of 48 cm² and a length of 8 cm. What is its perimeter?
items.e: Step 1: breadth = 48 ÷ 8 = 6 cm. Step 2: perimeter = 2 × (8 + 6) = 28 cm. (14 cm is only length + breadth.)

items.q: A rectangle has an area of 63 m² and a length of 9 m. What is its perimeter?
items.e: Step 1: breadth = 63 ÷ 9 = 7 m. Step 2: perimeter = 2 × (9 + 7) = 32 m. (16 m is only length + breadth.)

items.q: A rectangle has a perimeter of 36 cm and a length of 10 cm. What is its area?
items.e: Step 1: length + breadth = 36 ÷ 2 = 18, so breadth = 18 − 10 = 8 cm. Step 2: area = 10 × 8 = 80 cm². (160 comes from using 36 − 10 − 10 = 16 as the breadth without halving.)

items.q: A rectangle has a perimeter of 50 m and a length of 15 m. What is its area?
items.e: Step 1: length + breadth = 50 ÷ 2 = 25, so breadth = 25 − 15 = 10 m. Step 2: area = 15 × 10 = 150 m². (300 comes from using 50 − 15 − 15 = 20 as the breadth without halving.)

sets.title: Side of a square from its area or perimeter

items.q: The area of this square is 49 cm². How long is each side?
items.e: Side × side = 49. Use the multiplication table: 7 × 7 = 49, so each side is 7 cm. (Do not divide 49 by 4 or by 2: that is for a perimeter. 4 × 7 = 28 cm is the perimeter.)

items.q: The area of this square is 81 cm². How long is each side?
items.e: Side × side = 81. Use the multiplication table: 9 × 9 = 81, so each side is 9 cm. (Do not divide 81 by 4 or by 2: that is for a perimeter. 4 × 9 = 36 cm is the perimeter.)

items.q: The area of this square is 36 m². How long is each side?
items.e: Side × side = 36. Use the multiplication table: 6 × 6 = 36, so each side is 6 m. (Do not divide 36 by 4 or by 2: that is for a perimeter. 4 × 6 = 24 m is the perimeter.)

items.q: A square has an area of 25 m². How long is each side?
items.e: Side × side = 25. Use the multiplication table: 5 × 5 = 25, so each side is 5 m. (Do not divide 25 by 4 or by 2: that is for a perimeter. 4 × 5 = 20 m is the perimeter.)

items.q: A square has an area of 64 cm². How long is each side?
items.e: Side × side = 64. Use the multiplication table: 8 × 8 = 64, so each side is 8 cm. (Do not divide 64 by 4 or by 2: that is for a perimeter. 4 × 8 = 32 cm is the perimeter.)

items.q: A square has an area of 100 m². How long is each side?
items.e: Side × side = 100. Use the multiplication table: 10 × 10 = 100, so each side is 10 m. (Do not divide 100 by 4 or by 2: that is for a perimeter. 4 × 10 = 40 m is the perimeter.)

items.q: The perimeter of this square is 36 cm. How long is each side?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides: 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm. Check: 4 × 9 = 36. (36 ÷ 2 = 18 is two sides, not one.)

items.q: A square has a perimeter of 52 m. How long is each side?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides: 52 ÷ 4 = 13 m. Check: 4 × 13 = 52. (52 ÷ 2 = 26 is two sides, not one.)

items.q: A square has a perimeter of 80 cm. How long is each side?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides: 80 ÷ 4 = 20 cm. Check: 4 × 20 = 80. (80 ÷ 2 = 40 is two sides, not one.)

items.q: The perimeter of this square is 28 m. How long is each side?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides: 28 ÷ 4 = 7 m. Check: 4 × 7 = 28. (28 ÷ 2 = 14 is two sides, not one.)

items.q: A square has a perimeter of 100 cm. How long is each side?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides: 100 ÷ 4 = 25 cm. Check: 4 × 25 = 100. (100 ÷ 2 = 50 is two sides, not one.)

items.q: A square has a perimeter of 28 cm. What is its area?
items.e: Step 1: side = 28 ÷ 4 = 7 cm. Step 2: area = 7 × 7 = 49 cm². (196 uses half the perimeter, 14, as the side: halving instead of dividing by 4.)

items.q: A square garden has a perimeter of 40 m. What is its area?
items.e: Step 1: side = 40 ÷ 4 = 10 m. Step 2: area = 10 × 10 = 100 m². (400 uses half the perimeter, 20, as the side: halving instead of dividing by 4.)

items.q: A square tile has a perimeter of 32 cm. What is its area?
items.e: Step 1: side = 32 ÷ 4 = 8 cm. Step 2: area = 8 × 8 = 64 cm². (256 uses half the perimeter, 16, as the side: halving instead of dividing by 4.)

items.q: A piece of wire 48 cm long is bent to form a square. What is the area of the square?
items.e: Step 1: side = 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm. Step 2: area = 12 × 12 = 144 cm². (576 uses half the perimeter, 24, as the side: halving instead of dividing by 4.)

items.q: A square has an area of 64 cm². What is its perimeter?
items.e: Step 1: 8 × 8 = 64, so each side is 8 cm. Step 2: perimeter = 4 × 8 = 32 cm. (8 cm is only one side.)

items.q: A square has an area of 36 cm². What is its perimeter?
items.e: Step 1: 6 × 6 = 36, so each side is 6 cm. Step 2: perimeter = 4 × 6 = 24 cm. (6 cm is only one side.)

items.q: A square has an area of 81 m². What is its perimeter?
items.e: Step 1: 9 × 9 = 81, so each side is 9 m. Step 2: perimeter = 4 × 9 = 36 m. (9 m is only one side.)

items.q: A square has the same area as a rectangle 9 cm by 4 cm. How long is each side of the square?
items.e: Area of the rectangle = 9 × 4 = 36 cm². The square also has 36 cm², and 6 × 6 = 36, so each side is 6 cm. (6.5 cm would give the same perimeter, 26 cm, not the same area.)

items.q: A square and a rectangle both have a perimeter of 24 cm. The rectangle is 8 cm long. Which has the bigger area?
items.e: Square: side = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 cm, area = 36 cm². Rectangle: breadth = 12 − 8 = 4 cm, area = 8 × 4 = 32 cm². 36 − 32 = 4 cm². The same perimeter does not mean the same area.

sets.title: Composite figures: find the missing sides first

items.q: All the corners are right angles. What is the length of side x?
items.e: Look at the sides that run the same way as x. The whole side is 12 cm and the other part is 5 cm. x = 12 − 5 = 7 cm. (Using 12 cm for x takes the whole side, not the part.)

items.q: All the corners are right angles. What is the perimeter of the figure?
items.e: First find the missing sides: 10 − 4 = 6 and 2 + 5 = 7. Then add all 6 sides: 10 + 2 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 7 = 34 cm. (21 cm adds only the sides with numbers.) Shortcut: an L-shaped figure has the same perimeter as the rectangle round it: 2 × (10 + 7) = 34.

items.q: The figure is split into two rectangles. What is the area of the figure?
items.e: Split it into two rectangles: 10 × 3 = 30 cm² and 4 × 5 = 20 cm². 30 + 20 = 50 cm². (62 uses the whole side, 8 cm, for the second rectangle, so the overlap is counted twice.)

items.q: All the corners are right angles. What is the length of side x?
items.e: Look at the sides that run the same way as x. The whole side is 10 m and the other part is 3 m. x = 10 − 3 = 7 m. (Using 10 m for x takes the whole side, not the part.)

items.q: All the corners are right angles. What is the perimeter of the figure?
items.e: First find the missing sides: 15 − 6 = 9 and 4 + 7 = 11. Then add all 6 sides: 15 + 4 + 9 + 7 + 6 + 11 = 52 m. (32 m adds only the sides with numbers.) Shortcut: an L-shaped figure has the same perimeter as the rectangle round it: 2 × (15 + 11) = 52.

items.q: The figure is split into two rectangles. What is the area of the figure?
items.e: Split it into two rectangles: 12 × 4 = 48 m² and 5 × 5 = 25 m². 48 + 25 = 73 m². (93 uses the whole side, 9 m, for the second rectangle, so the overlap is counted twice.)

items.q: All the corners are right angles. What is the length of side x?
items.e: Look at the sides that run the same way as x. The whole side is 8 cm and the other part is 5 cm. x = 8 − 5 = 3 cm. (Using 8 cm for x takes the whole side, not the part.)

items.q: All the corners are right angles. What is the perimeter of the figure?
items.e: First find the missing sides: 13 − 8 = 5 and 6 + 3 = 9. Then add all 6 sides: 8 + 6 + 5 + 3 + 13 + 9 = 44 cm. (30 cm adds only the sides with numbers.) Shortcut: an L-shaped figure has the same perimeter as the rectangle round it: 2 × (13 + 9) = 44.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm by 1 cm. What is the area of the shaded figure?
items.e: Split it into two rectangles: 5 × 5 = 25 and 3 × 3 = 9. 25 + 9 = 34 cm². (40 cm² counts the empty corner too; 26 cm is the perimeter.)

items.q: All the corners are right angles. What is the area of the figure?
items.e: First, the missing side is 7 − 3 = 4 cm. Split it into two rectangles: 9 × 3 = 27 cm² and 4 × 4 = 16 cm². 27 + 16 = 43 cm². (55 uses the whole side, 7 cm, for the second rectangle, so the overlap is counted twice.)

items.q: All the corners are right angles. What is the length of side x?
items.e: Look at the sides that run the same way as x. The whole side is 13 cm and the other parts are 5 cm and 4 cm, which make 9 cm. x = 13 − 9 = 4 cm. (Using 13 cm for x takes the whole side, not the part.)

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm by 1 cm. What is the perimeter of the shaded figure?
items.e: Count the 1-cm sides all round: 7 + 6 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 6 = 32 cm. (26 cm is the rectangle round it, which misses the two 3-cm sides inside the gap; 33 is the number of squares, the area.)

items.q: All the corners are right angles. What is the perimeter of the figure?
items.e: First find the missing sides: 14 − (4 + 5) = 5 and (6 + 4) − 4 = 6. Then add all 8 sides: 14 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 4 + 6 + 5 + 4 = 48 cm. (37 cm adds only the sides with numbers.)

items.q: All the corners are right angles. What is the area of the figure?
items.e: Take the missing corner away from the big rectangle: 14 × 10 = 140 m², and the corner is 8 × 6 = 48 m². 140 − 48 = 92 m². Or split it into two rectangles: 56 + 36 = 92. (140 m² is the whole big rectangle.)

items.q: The figure is split into two rectangles. What is the area of the figure?
items.e: Top bar: 12 × 3 = 36 cm². Stem: 4 × 6 = 24 cm² (its height is 9 − 3 = 6). 36 + 24 = 60 cm². (72 uses the whole height, 9 cm, for the stem and counts the overlap twice.)

items.q: All the corners are right angles. What is the area of the figure?
items.e: Take the missing corner away from the big rectangle: 11 × 9 = 99 cm², and the corner is 6 × 5 = 30 cm². 99 − 30 = 69 cm². Or split it into two rectangles: 44 + 25 = 69. (99 cm² is the whole big rectangle.)

items.q: The figure is made of a square of side 6 cm and a square of side 4 cm. What is its perimeter?
items.e: Go round the outside: 6 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 10 + 6 = 32 cm. (40 cm adds both perimeters, 24 + 16, and counts the 4-cm line where the squares touch twice. 52 cm² is the area.)

items.q: All the corners are right angles. What is the area of the figure?
items.e: Top bar: 15 × 4 = 60 m². Stem: 5 × 6 = 30 m² (its height is 10 − 4 = 6). 60 + 30 = 90 m². (110 uses the whole height, 10 m, for the stem and counts the overlap twice.)

items.q: The figure is made of a square of side 7 m and a square of side 5 m. What is its area?
items.e: Big square: 7 × 7 = 49 m². Small square: 5 × 5 = 25 m². 49 + 25 = 74 m². (84 m² is the whole 12 m by 7 m rectangle round it; 35 m² multiplies the two numbers shown, 7 × 5; 49 m² is only the big square.)

items.q: A rectangle 10 cm by 8 cm has a 3 cm by 2 cm piece cut from one corner, making an L-shaped figure. Which is true?
c: The area is smaller and the perimeter is longer
Both the area and the perimeter are smaller
The area is smaller but the perimeter is the same
The area and the perimeter stay the same
items.e: Area: 80 − 6 = 74 cm², smaller. Perimeter: the two new sides inside the corner (3 cm and 2 cm) replace the 3 cm and 2 cm that were cut off, so it stays 36 cm.

sets.title: Word problems: fencing, tiles and paths

items.q: Mr Tan’s community garden plot is 15 m long and 9 m wide. He puts a fence all round it. How long is the fence?
items.e: A fence goes round the edge, so find the perimeter: 2 × (15 + 9) = 2 × 24 = 48 m. (135 is the area; 24 m goes only halfway; 39 m leaves out one side.)

items.q: A rectangular playground at a void deck is 18 m long and 12 m wide. A fence goes all round it, except for a gate 2 m wide. How long is the fence?
items.e: Perimeter = 2 × (18 + 12) = 60 m. Take away the gate: 60 − 2 = 58 m. (62 m adds the gate instead.)

items.q: Arjun’s family fences a rectangular herb garden 10 m long and 6 m wide. The fencing costs $12 per metre. How much does the fencing cost?
items.e: Fence = perimeter = 2 × (10 + 6) = 32 m. Cost = 32 × $12 = $384. ($720 uses the area, 60 m², $192 uses only 16 m, and $44 adds 32 + 12.)

items.q: A rectangular notice board is 120 cm long and 80 cm wide. It is covered with square cards of side 20 cm, with no gaps. How many cards are needed?
items.e: Along the length: 120 ÷ 20 = 6 cards. Along the breadth: 80 ÷ 20 = 4 cards. 6 × 4 = 24 cards. (480 divides the area by the side, 9600 ÷ 20; 10 adds 6 + 4.)

items.q: Mrs Ng’s living room floor is 5 m long and 4 m wide. She covers it with square tiles of side 50 cm. How many tiles does she need?
items.e: Change to centimetres: 500 cm by 400 cm. 500 ÷ 50 = 10 tiles along, 400 ÷ 50 = 8 tiles across. 10 × 8 = 80 tiles. (20 is the number of 1-m tiles; 18 adds 10 + 8.)

items.q: A square courtyard has an area of 64 m². It is paved with square tiles of side 2 m. How many tiles are needed?
items.e: One tile covers 2 × 2 = 4 m². 64 ÷ 4 = 16 tiles. Or: each side is 8 m, so 4 tiles along and 4 across. (32 divides by the side, 2, instead of by the area of a tile, 4.)

items.q: A kitchen wall is 3 m long and 2 m high. Tiles for it cost $15 per square metre. How much do the tiles cost?
items.e: Area = 3 × 2 = 6 m². Cost = 6 × $15 = $90. ($150 uses the perimeter, 10 m; $75 uses 3 + 2 = 5.)

items.q: A garden 12 m by 8 m has a path 1 m wide all round it. What is the area of the path?
items.e: Garden and path together: (12 + 1 + 1) × (8 + 1 + 1) = 14 × 10 = 140 m². Garden: 12 × 8 = 96 m². Path: 140 − 96 = 44 m². (40 m² leaves out the 4 corner squares of the path.)

items.q: A school field is 20 m long and 12 m wide. Two paths, each 2 m wide, cross it as shown. The rest of the field is grass. What is the area of the grass?
items.e: Slide the four grass pieces together: (20 − 2) × (12 − 2) = 18 × 10 = 180 m². (176 m² takes away 40 m² and 24 m², which counts the 2 m by 2 m square where the paths cross twice. 200 m² and 216 m² take away only one path.)

items.q: The length of a rectangle is 3 times its breadth. Its perimeter is 64 cm. What is its area?
items.e: Length + breadth = 64 ÷ 2 = 32 cm. In the model this is 4 units, so 1 unit = 32 ÷ 4 = 8 cm. Breadth = 8 cm, length = 3 × 8 = 24 cm. Area = 24 × 8 = 192 cm². (768 cm² comes from 4 units = 64, forgetting to halve the perimeter.)

items.q: A rectangular badminton practice area has a perimeter of 50 m. Its length is 5 m longer than its breadth. What is its length?
items.e: Length + breadth = 50 ÷ 2 = 25 m. Take away the extra 5 m: 25 − 5 = 20 m = 2 units, so 1 unit = 10 m. Breadth = 10 m, length = 10 + 5 = 15 m. (20 m is 2 units, not the length; 12.5 m is 25 ÷ 2, which leaves out the extra 5 m; 22.5 m comes from (50 − 5) ÷ 2.)

items.q: A wire 60 cm long is cut into two pieces, A and B. Piece A is twice as long as piece B. Each piece is bent to make a square. How long is each side of the smaller square?
items.e: 3 units = 60 cm, so 1 unit = 20 cm. Piece B is 20 cm, the perimeter of the smaller square. Side = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cm. (20 cm is the whole piece; 10 cm halves it instead of dividing by 4; 15 cm is 60 ÷ 4.)

items.q: Priya’s square garden has the same area as a rectangular garden 16 m by 4 m. How much fence does she need to go round her square garden?
items.e: Area = 16 × 4 = 64 m². 8 × 8 = 64, so each side is 8 m. Fence = 4 × 8 = 32 m. (40 m is the fence for the rectangular garden.)

items.q: Students paint a mural on a wall 5 m long and 3 m high for National Day. A door 2 m high and 1 m wide in the wall is not painted. What area do they paint?
items.e: Wall: 5 × 3 = 15 m². Door: 2 × 1 = 2 m². 15 − 2 = 13 m². (17 m² adds the door instead of taking it away; 16 m is the perimeter of the wall.)

items.q: Raju’s bedroom floor in an HDB flat is 6 m long and 5 m wide. A rug 4 m by 3 m lies on it. What area of the floor is not covered?
items.e: Floor: 6 × 5 = 30 m². Rug: 4 × 3 = 12 m². 30 − 12 = 18 m². (4 m² comes from (6 − 4) × (5 − 3), taking away the sides instead of the areas.)

items.q: A rectangular card is 30 cm by 20 cm. A square of side 5 cm is cut from each of its 4 corners. What area of card is left?
items.e: Card: 30 × 20 = 600 cm². One corner square: 5 × 5 = 25 cm². Four corners: 4 × 25 = 100 cm². 600 − 100 = 500 cm². (575 takes away only one square; 580 takes away 4 × 5, the sides, not the areas.)

items.q: A rectangular card is 30 cm by 20 cm. A square of side 5 cm is cut from each of its 4 corners. What is the perimeter of the card that is left?
items.e: At each corner, two 5-cm sides are cut off and two new 5-cm sides go in. So the perimeter stays 2 × (30 + 20) = 100 cm. (80 cm takes away 4 × 5; 140 cm adds 8 × 5.)

items.q: Xin Yi makes a square Teachers’ Day card with an area of 81 cm². She glues ribbon all round its edge. How much ribbon does she need?
items.e: 9 × 9 = 81, so each side is 9 cm. Ribbon = perimeter = 4 × 9 = 36 cm. (324 cm is 4 × 81, using the area as a side.)

items.q: Mr Rahman builds a rectangular pen for his chickens against a wall. The wall is one length, 14 m, so it needs no fence. He uses 30 m of fencing for the other three sides. What is the breadth of the pen?
items.e: The fence covers 1 length + 2 breadths. 30 − 14 = 16 m for the 2 breadths, so 1 breadth = 16 ÷ 2 = 8 m. (15 m halves the whole 30 m; 1 m comes from fencing all four sides: 30 ÷ 2 − 14.)

items.q: The school field is 80 m long and 50 m wide. During PE, Hafiz runs round the edge of the field 3 times. How far does he run?
items.e: Once round = perimeter = 2 × (80 + 50) = 260 m. 3 times: 3 × 260 = 780 m. (390 m uses half the perimeter; 12 000 uses the area.)
